```{=html}
<details
  id="report-methodology"
  class="method-note method-details report-tab-panel"
  data-report-tab="intro"
>
  <summary>How this report works</summary>
  <div class="method-details-content">
    <p><strong>Combined report scope.</strong> The supplied <code>prsc_id</code> identifies the user's imputation context. The report then takes the latest completed result for each PGS across all PRS jobs belonging to that imputation and assigns it to the section defined by <code>pgs_reports_shop.report_name</code>.</p>
    <p><strong>Overall profile index.</strong> The whole-report index is the arithmetic mean of the displayed trait percentiles, with every trait receiving equal weight. It is shown as a compact 0–100 reference value and is a descriptive profile summary, not a combined clinical-risk score.</p>
    <p><strong>Ancestry adjustment and validation evidence.</strong> The report separates two related ancestry tasks. First, the displayed genetic percentile is normalized continuously across genetic ancestry. The reader-facing <strong>Mean-adjusted</strong> value corresponds to adjustment of ancestry-related differences in the mean score, while <strong>Ancestry-standardized</strong> additionally adjusts ancestry-related differences in score variance and is the primary report value. This continuous adjustment is especially useful when a person is admixed or does not lie cleanly inside one labeled reference population. Second, validation cohorts are selected from every ancestry component above 20%, with the recorded primary ancestry retained as a fallback. This means a substantially admixed person can retain evaluation evidence from more than one ancestry group. The ESS field can contain several comma-separated ancestry labels, so recognized ancestry tokens are matched rather than requiring the full field to equal one label. The selected cohort identifiers then restrict the performance evaluations considered for each polygenic score. No ancestry adjustment can fully compensate for sparse reference data, so results remain dependent on reference-panel diversity and sample size.</p>
    <p><strong>Evidence labels.</strong> Model agreement and validation-performance badges use an ordered low-to-high scale rather than value-laden terms such as good or bad. These labels describe statistical consistency or discrimination, not whether the user's health result is favorable.</p>
    <p><strong>Card summary text.</strong> Each card currently includes a generic plain-language box that combines the personalized percentile interpretation with a temporary explanation of the trait and the statistics shown in the card. This text is designed to be replaced by curated, database-backed trait descriptions.</p>
    <p><strong>Report presentation.</strong> The interactive HTML report uses one Introduction tab plus one tab for each health section defined by <code>pgs_reports_shop.report_name</code>. Each health tab contains its own short category introduction and category-specific “Your profile at a glance” summary; no whole-report percentile spectrum is used because combining hundreds of traits makes the visualization difficult to interpret. Only the selected tab is shown on screen, while printing reveals all sections sequentially. Within each health tab, results at or above the 80th percentile and below the 20th percentile are rendered as full result cards. Results from the 20th through 79th percentile are shown in a compact expandable list with a single technical summary table rather than repeating the full card and two large evidence tables for every ordinary result. This changes presentation only; it does not change score inclusion or percentile calculation.</p>
    <p><strong>Report sections, card grouping, and performance-evaluation representation.</strong> Every scored PGS is first assigned to the health section named by <code>pgs_reports_shop.report_name</code>. Card clustering then occurs only within that section. Within a section, polygenic scores are clustered into cards using an explicit curated trait-family override when one is configured, followed by two general links: an ontology-aware key derived from <code>pgscatalog_data.efo_id</code>, and an exact match of the trimmed <code>reported_trait</code> text. Curated overrides take precedence over ontology matching so a known broad or incorrect ontology assignment cannot pull an unrelated score into the card. Outside the curated overrides, a match by either general route joins the scores and the links are applied transitively. When one or more MONDO identifiers are present, the MONDO subset defines the ontology key and accompanying EFO, HP, or PATO terms are treated as contextual modifiers. Without MONDO, PATO modifiers are ignored when another ontology identifier remains. Multiple core identifiers are preserved as an unordered set for genuinely composite endpoints. When ontology IDs are unavailable, the mapped EFO label can still provide the ontology-side link. The visible card title remains a human-readable <code>pgscatalog_data.reported_trait</code> selected from the primary PGS in the resulting card cluster. The ancestry-standardized percentile, z-score, variant match, and model agreement are represented once per polygenic score because they are properties of the user's score result rather than of an individual performance row. By contrast, odds-ratio and hazard-ratio plots retain every ancestry-matched performance evaluation that reports the corresponding effect, so more-stratified outcomes from <code>pgs_performance.reported_trait</code> remain visible. The Scores orb counts distinct retained PGS IDs with a displayed ancestry-standardized percentile. The Effects orb counts the OR and HR estimates actually plotted; a performance evaluation that reports both contributes one estimate to each plot. The Cohorts orb counts distinct cohort names only after restricting the evidence table to the final retained PGS IDs for the card. The Publications orb counts distinct performance-publication IDs (PGP IDs, with PMID/DOI fallbacks) from those same retained ancestry-matched performance records; development publications are not used as a fallback for this count. The technical dropdown separately reports the total number of ancestry-matched performance evaluations, including records without OR or HR.</p>
    <p><strong>Validation discrimination.</strong> AUROC and concordance are optional descriptive evidence rather than score-eligibility requirements. When available, ancestry-matched performance evaluations contribute one discrimination value per record: AUROC is used when reported, otherwise the concordance statistic. A score with no AUROC or concordance can still remain in the report when it has ancestry-matched evaluation evidence and passes variant-match QC.</p>
    <p><strong>Model selection.</strong> The only hard score-level pruning in this report is ancestry relevance plus variant match: PGS models with less than 70% matched variants or missing variant-match data are removed before model agreement, overview figures, or card construction. AUROC and concordance do not determine inclusion. When selecting the representative primary PGS for a card, available discrimination is used as a ranking preference, followed by evaluation sample size; models without discrimination remain eligible.</p>
    <p><strong>Model families and SNPster weighted effects.</strong> Within each development publication and reported trait, scores with the same non-missing development method receive the same descriptive family ID. For odds- and hazard-based plots only, the SNPster weighted mean uses raw weight <code>(1 / family size) × performance-record AUROC or concordance × variant-match fraction</code>. Percentile summaries remain unweighted.</p>
    <p><strong>Model agreement.</strong> Agreement is calculated from the ancestry-standardized percentiles. For cards with more than four retained percentile values, agreement is classified from IQR width. For cards with two to four values, agreement uses the full minimum-to-maximum distance. Spread below 5 percentile points is Very high agreement, below 10 is High, below 20 is Moderate, 20–25 is Low, and above 25 is Very low. A single retained PGS is Not assessable.</p>
    <p><strong>Distribution display.</strong> Multi-PGS percentile cards use ancestry-standardized percentiles and show the IQR as the translucent band and Tukey whiskers as the skinny colored line. PGS points are colored by development publication, while odds/hazard estimate points are colored by validation publication; the same publication receives the same deterministic color throughout the report. Odds and hazard bars are centered on 0% change and show between-model spread rather than statistical confidence intervals.</p>
  </div>
</details>
```

```{=html}
<div
  class="method-note report-tab-panel"
  data-report-tab="intro"
>
  <strong>Important limitations.</strong>
  Polygenic scores estimate inherited genetic predisposition; they are not diagnostic tests.
  AUROC/concordance summaries, odds ratios, and hazard ratios come from ancestry-matched cohort-level performance records and may still not transfer perfectly across age groups, sex, genotyping arrays, imputation pipelines, or more fine-grained ancestry differences.
  The individualized risk-effect calculation uses the user's ancestry-standardized z-score and assumes that the source odds ratio or hazard ratio is reported per standard deviation of the PRS. If the original publication used a different effect unit or comparison group, the transformed percentage may be misleading and should be flagged in your score-selection database.
</div>
```
